newsitem.title: USA: Hearings challenge the "light" in cigarette brands.
newsitem.headline: Hearings challenge the "light" in cigarette brands.

text.p: Cigarette smokers are getting as much as twice the tar and nocotine they expect when smoking so-called light or ultra-light cigarettes, according to testimony Thursday at a public hearing on cigarette contents.

"Unfortunately, those consumers are not getting what they pay for. They are getting a lot more (tar and nicotine) than they pay for," Jack Henningfield, a Johns Hopkins Medical School researcher, told a Massachusetts Department of Public Health panel.

The Massachusetts Department of Public Health hearings are part of a process to design regulations that will require all companies that sell cigarettes and smokeless tobacco in the state to disclose the ingredients by brand by July 1.

Two-thirds of the cigarettes sold in the United States fall into what the tobacco industry calls light or ultra-light categories and most consumers belive that means less tar and nicotine, Henningfield said.
The department also released a report it commissioned from a Canadian laboratory that compared 10 common U.S. cigarette brands.

The Kitchener, Ontario-based Labstat Inc. report measured tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide. Using National Cancer Institute test standards, the lab broke the tests into two segments, mimicking average smoking and intense smoking.
The results showed smokers were getting about double the nicotine and tar as compared with standards developed by the Federal Trade Commission and used by tobacco companies.
David Remes, a Washington lawyer who represents four major tobacco companies, said he was not surprised by the findings.
"The ratings are not meant to translate intake of nicotine or tar, but allow smokers to distinguish one brand from another," he said.
"Practically everything said this morning has been said a million times... It makes good theatre but doesn't have much to do with implementing the statute," Remes said.

The four firms challenging the constitutionality of the Massachusetts law in federal court are: Philip Morris Cos. Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc and Lorillard Tobacco Co., a unit of Loews Corp.
Efforts by the four companies to block the hearings failed Wednesday when a federal judge ruled the hearings could go on as planned.
